concepts.title: Gabor Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Gabor transform is the result of varying the central frequency of a Gabor function applied to an image, analogous to a Fourier transform with a Gaussian window.
concepts.content:
The convolution with a Gabor function is equivalent to performing a Fourier transform of the image after applying a Gaussian window. If we write the convolution in detail:
$$\begin{split}
\ell_{\psi} \left(x,y,u,v \right)  & =   \iint \ell\left(x',y'\right) \psi(x-x',y-y';u,v) \, dx' dy' = \\
& = \iint  \ell\left(x',y'\right) g(x-x',y-y') \exp \left( j \left(u (x-x') + v (y-y') \right) \right) dx' dy' = \\
\end{split}$$
By extracting the term independent of $(x',y')$ and using the symmetry of the Gaussian window, we obtain:
$$\begin{split}
& = \exp \left( j \left(u x + v y \right) \right) \iint \ell\left(x',y'\right) g(x'-x,y'-y) \exp \left(- j \left(u x' + v y' \right) \right) dx' dy'
\end{split}$$
The Gabor transform is obtained when we vary the central frequency $(u,v)$ of the Gabor function. Note that the Gabor transform is not self-inverting.
concepts.motivation_md: The Gabor transform provides a way to analyze local frequency content within an image. While a standard Fourier transform gives global frequency information, the Gabor transform uses a Gaussian window to localize the analysis, allowing for a joint representation of spatial and frequency information.
concepts.recap_md: - It acts as a Fourier transform applied after a Gaussian windowing of the image.

concepts.title: Steerable Filters
concepts.one_liner: Steerable filters allow the synthesis of a filter at any orientation as a linear combination of a fixed set of basis filters.
concepts.content:
Steerable filters address the problem of transforming a filter $h(x,y)$ into a continuous function $h(x,y, \theta)$ of angle $\theta$. Instead of creating a new function for every orientation, we can interpolate between a fixed number of predefined oriented filter outputs. 

A simple example is the Gaussian derivative. We can synthesize a directional derivative in any direction as a linear combination of horizontal and vertical derivatives. The steering equation for the first derivative of a Gaussian filter is:
$$g_{x}(x,y,\theta) = \cos(\theta) g_x(x,y) + \sin(\theta) g_y(x,y)$$
where $g_x$ and $g_y$ are the Gaussian derivatives along $x$ and $y$, and the interpolation functions are $k_1(\theta) = \cos(\theta)$ and $k_2(\theta) = \sin(\theta)$.

For second-order Gaussian derivatives, the steering equation requires three basis filters:
$$\begin{split}
g_{x,x}(x,y,\theta) & = g_{xx}(\cos(\theta) x - \sin (\theta) y, \sin(\theta) x + \cos (\theta)y) = \\
 &= \cos^2(\theta) g_{xx}(x,y) + \sin^2(\theta) g_{yy}(x,y) - 2 \cos(\theta) \sin(\theta) g_{xy}(x,y) 
\end{split}$$
The interpolation functions are $k_1(\theta) = \cos^2(\theta)$, $k_2(\theta) = \sin^2(\theta)$, and $k_3(\theta) = -2\cos(\theta)\sin(\theta)$.

This leads to an architecture where input images pass through a set of basis filters, and the outputs are modulated with gain maps to steer the filter to desired orientations at each position.

(see figure: Architecture for steerable filters. This architecture computes the second-order image derivative along orientation $\theta$.)
concepts.motivation_md: In image processing, it is often necessary to analyze features at many different orientations. Computing a full convolution for every possible angle is computationally expensive. Steerable filters solve this by allowing any orientation to be synthesized from a small, fixed set of basis filters.
concepts.recap_md: - Any orientation can be synthesized via a linear combination of basis filters.

key_passage.text: The input images pass through a set of basis filters, then the outputs of those filters are modulated with a set of gain maps (which can be different at each pixel). Those gain maps adjust the linear combinations of the basis filters to allow the input filter to be steered to the desired orientations at each position.

concepts.title: Orientation sampling and interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Orientation sampling is a generalization of the Nyquist sampling theorem applied to the angular dimension of filters.
concepts.content: Orientation sampling and interpolation is a generalization of the Nyquist sampling theorem applied to dimensions other than space. Just as the Nyquist theorem applies to spatial sampling, we can ask if a certain number of discrete samples in orientation allows one to interpolate and synthesize the response of a filter at any arbitrary, intermediate orientation. The answer is yes, and the specific number of filter samples required for successful interpolation depends on the mathematical form of the filter.
concepts.motivation_md: To efficiently process images with oriented filters, we need to know the minimum number of discrete orientations required to perfectly reconstruct the filter's response at any other angle, preventing redundant computations.
concepts.recap_md: - It applies Nyquist-like sampling principles to the orientation of filters.

key_passage.text: given a certain number of discrete samples in orientation (or space), can one interpolate between the samples and synthesize what would have been found from having a filter (or a spatial sample) at some arbitrary, intermediate orientation? The answer is yes, and the number of filter samples needed to interpolate depends on the form of the filter.

concepts.title: Steering Theorem
concepts.one_liner: The Steering Theorem quantifies the number of basis filters required to synthesize a rotated version of a filter based on its angular frequency content.
concepts.content:
The Steering Theorem quantifies how many basis filters are needed to steer a given filter $h(x,y)$. For a filter expressed in polar coordinates as $h(r,\phi)$, the steering condition requires that the rotated filter $h(r,\phi - \theta)$ be a linear combination of a set of basis filters $h(r,\phi - \theta_m)$:
$$h(r,\phi - \theta) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} k_{m}(\theta) h(r,\phi - \theta_m) .$$
If the filter is expressed as a Fourier series in angle:
$$h(r,\phi) = \sum_{n=-N}^{N} a_n(r) \exp \left( j n \phi \right)$$
then the steering condition holds if and only if the interpolation functions $k_{j}(\theta)$ satisfy the following matrix equation:
$$\left[
\begin{array}{c}
1 \\
\exp (j \theta) \\
\ldots \\
\exp (j N \theta) \\
\end{array}
\right]
=
\left[ 
\begin{array}{cccc}
1 & 1 & \ldots & 1 \\
\exp (j \theta_{1}) & \exp (j \theta_{2}) & \ldots & \exp (j \theta_{M}) \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
\exp (j N \theta_{1}) & \exp (j N \theta_{2}) & \ldots & \exp (j N \theta_{M})
\end{array}
\right]
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
k_{1}(\theta) \\ k_{2}(\theta) \\ \vdots \\ k_{M}(\theta) 
\end{array}
\right].$$
concepts.motivation_md: The theorem provides the mathematical foundation for determining exactly how many basis functions are needed to represent a filter at any rotation, which depends on the filter's angular complexity.
concepts.recap_md: - The number of basis filters depends on the filter's Fourier series expansion in angle.

key_passage.text: The steering condition is the requirement that the rotated filter, h(r,φ - θ), be a linear combination of a set of basis filters that are rotated versions of itself, h(r,φ - θ_m) with m ∈ (1,M).

concepts.title: Steering Condition
concepts.one_liner: The steering condition is the requirement that a rotated filter can be expressed as a linear combination of a fixed set of basis filters.
concepts.content:
Consider a filter with impulse response $h(x,y)$, written in polar coordinates as $h(r,\phi)$. The steering condition is the requirement that the rotated filter, $h(r,\phi - \theta)$, be a linear combination of a set of basis filters that are rotated versions of itself, $h(r,\phi - \theta_m)$ with $m \in (1,M)$. The steering condition is expressed as:
$$h(r,\phi - \theta) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} k_{m}(\theta) h(r,\phi - \theta_m) .$$
concepts.motivation_md: This condition defines the fundamental property a filter must satisfy to be considered 'steerable,' enabling efficient rotation through interpolation.
concepts.recap_md: - It defines a rotated filter as a weighted sum of fixed basis rotations.

concepts.title: Basis Functions for Polynomial Filters
concepts.one_liner: For $N$-th order polynomial filters with even or odd symmetry, $N+1$ basis functions are sufficient for steerability.
concepts.content: It is often convenient to treat filters as polynomials multiplied by radially symmetric window functions, such as high-order Gaussian derivatives. In these cases, it can be shown that for an $N$-th order polynomial with even or odd symmetry, $N+1$ basis functions are sufficient to achieve steerability.
concepts.motivation_md: This provides a simple rule of thumb for determining the complexity of steerable implementations for common polynomial-based filters like Gaussian derivatives.
concepts.recap_md: - $N+1$ basis functions are enough for $N$-th order symmetric polynomial filters.

concepts.title: Steerability and Sampling
concepts.one_liner: Steerability is a property that is preserved even after the filter function has been spatially sampled.
concepts.content: Although steerability is typically derived in the continuous domain, the property still holds after sampling the filter function. This is because spatial sampling and steerability are interchangeable: the weighted sum of a spatially sampled function is equal to the spatial sampling of the same weighted sum of continuous basis functions.
concepts.motivation_md: This ensures that the theoretical benefits of steerable filters translate perfectly to digital implementations where signals and filters are discrete.
concepts.recap_md: - Spatial sampling and steerability are interchangeable operations.

concepts.title: Separable Basis Filters
concepts.one_liner: Using $x-y$ separable functions as basis filters improves computational efficiency in steerable filter architectures.
concepts.content: For computational efficiency, it is advantageous to have basis filters that are $x-y$ separable functions. In many cases, such basis functions are easy to find. When they are not readily apparent, simple numerical methods can be employed to find the best-fitting $x-y$ separable basis set.
concepts.motivation_md: Separable filters significantly reduce the number of operations required for convolution, making real-time steerable filter banks more feasible.
concepts.recap_md: - Separable basis filters are preferred for computational speed.

concepts.title: Localization property of Gabor functions
concepts.one_liner: Gabor functions are the optimal functions for achieving the best simultaneous localization in both the spatial and frequency domains.
concepts.content: Gabor functions are localized in both the spatial and frequency domain. One remarkable property of the Gabor function is that it is the optimal function that achieves the best simultaneous localization in space and frequency.
concepts.motivation_md: In signal processing, there is an inherent trade-off between precision in time (or space) and precision in frequency. Gabor functions are fundamental because they reach the theoretical limit of this uncertainty principle, providing the most efficient possible representation for localized features.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gabor functions provide simultaneous localization in spatial and frequency domains.
- They are mathematically optimal for achieving the best possible joint localization.

concepts.title: Quadrature Phase
concepts.one_liner: Quadrature phase describes pairs of filters whose impulse responses are Hilbert transform pairs, allowing for the measurement of local oriented energy.
concepts.content:
Pairs of filters can be in a relationship to each other called quadrature phase. This relationship is useful for many low-level visual processing tasks. When in quadrature phase, pairs of oriented filters can measure local oriented energy, identify contours independently of their phase, and measure positional changes very accurately.

Two band-pass filters are said to be in quadrature if their impulse responses are Hilbert transform pairs along some orientation in the frequency domain. Sine and cosine functions of the same frequency are Hilbert transform pairs, as are sine and cosine phase Gabor functions of the same frequency and Gaussian envelope parameters. Thus, these filter pairs are also quadrature pairs. When convolving two filters in quadrature with a signal (or image), the two outputs are also in quadrature.

The quadrature in Gabor functions is an approximation that only holds for $\sigma$ sufficiently large. For small $\sigma$, the filter does not form a quadrature pair. For large $\sigma$, the real and imaginary parts of the Gabor filter (cosine and sine phase local filters) are filters in quadrature with the vector $n=(u_0,v_0)$ pointing in the direction of the central frequency of the Gabor function.
concepts.motivation_md: Quadrature phase allows vision systems to detect features like edges and bars regardless of their specific phase (e.g., whether an edge goes from light-to-dark or dark-to-light), which is essential for robust contour detection and energy measurement.
concepts.recap_md:
- Filters in quadrature are Hilbert transform pairs along a specific orientation.
- This relationship allows for phase-invariant feature detection and accurate positional measurements.
- For Gabor filters, the quadrature relationship is an approximation that requires a sufficiently large $\sigma$.

concepts.title: Hilbert Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Hilbert transform is a technique used to create quadrature pairs by shifting the phase of frequency components by $\pm j$ based on their sign.
concepts.content:
For notational simplicity, quadrature pair filters are described in the time domain, but they extend naturally to two or more dimensions. Consider an even symmetric zero-mean signal, $\ell(t)$, with Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}(\omega)$, where $\mathscr{L}(0)=0$. In the Fourier domain, two functions, $\mathscr{L}(\omega)$ and $\mathscr{L}_h(\omega)$, are said to be Hilbert transform pairs if:

$$\mathscr{L}_h(\omega) = \begin{cases} - j \mathscr{L}(\omega) & \text{if } \omega >0 \\ j \mathscr{L}(\omega) & \text{if } \omega <0 \end{cases}$$

We define the complex signal as $\ell_a(t) = \ell(t) + j \ell_h(t)$. The extension of the Hilbert transform to images can be done in several ways. The most common approach in image processing is to define one direction, $n$, in the frequency space, resulting in the following transform:

$$\mathscr{L}_h(\omega_x,\omega_y) = \begin{cases} - j \mathscr{L}(\omega_x,\omega_y) & \text{if } n^T \cdot (\omega_x,\omega_y) > 0 \\ j \mathscr{L}(\omega_x,\omega_y) & \text{if } n^T \cdot (\omega_x,\omega_y) <0 \end{cases}$$
concepts.motivation_md: The Hilbert transform is the mathematical tool used to generate a 'companion' signal that is $90^\circ$ out of phase with the original. This is necessary for constructing analytic signals and measuring local energy in images.
concepts.recap_md:
- The Hilbert transform shifts the phase of a signal's frequency components by $90^\circ$.
- In 2D, it is defined relative to a specific direction $n$ in frequency space.
- It is used to form complex signals that combine even and odd symmetric components.

\end{cases}$$

\end{cases}$$
slots.example:
For notational simplicity, quadrature pair filters are described in the time domain, but they extend naturally to two or more dimensions. Consider an even symmetric zero-mean signal, $\ell(t)$, with Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}(\omega)$, where $\mathscr{L}(0)=0$. In the Fourier domain, two functions, $\mathscr{L}(\omega)$ and $\mathscr{L}_h(\omega)$, are said to be Hilbert transform pairs if:

$$\mathscr{L}_h(\omega) = \begin{cases} - j \mathscr{L}(\omega) & \text{if } \omega >0 \\ j \mathscr{L}(\omega) & \text{if } \omega <0 \end{cases}$$

We define the complex signal as $\ell_a(t) = \ell(t) + j \ell_h(t)$. The extension of the Hilbert transform to images can be done in several ways. The most common approach in image processing is to define one direction, $n$, in the frequency space, resulting in the following transform:

$$\mathscr{L}_h(\omega_x,\omega_y) = \begin{cases} - j \mathscr{L}(\omega_x,\omega_y) & \text{if } n^T \cdot (\omega_x,\omega_y) > 0 \\ j \mathscr{L}(\omega_x,\omega_y) & \text{if } n^T \cdot (\omega_x,\omega_y) <0 \end{cases}$$

concepts.title: Analytic Signal
concepts.one_liner: An analytic signal is a complex signal formed by a real signal and its Hilbert transform, containing no negative frequency components.
concepts.content:
The signal $\ell_a(t) = \ell(t) + j \ell_h(t)$, where $\ell_h(t)$ is the Hilbert transform of $\ell(t)$, is called the analytic signal. Its Fourier transform has no negative frequency components, such that:

$$\mathscr{L}_a(\omega) = \begin{cases} 2\mathscr{L}(\omega) & \text{if } \omega >0 \\ 0 & \text{if } \omega <0 \end{cases}$$

It is useful to write the complex signal $\ell_a(t)$ in polar form:

$$\ell_a(t) = a(t) \exp \left( j \, \theta (t) \right)$$

where $a(t)$ is the instantaneous amplitude (local amplitude) and $\theta (t)$ is the instantaneous phase (local phase). This representation is common in communications theory and is used to build image representations invariant to certain image structures.
concepts.motivation_md: By removing negative frequencies and representing a signal in complex polar form, we can separate the 'strength' of a signal (amplitude) from its 'structure' (phase), which is vital for modulation and feature analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- The analytic signal is formed by $\ell(t) + j \ell_h(t)$ and lacks negative frequencies.
- It can be expressed in polar form to reveal local amplitude and local phase.
- This representation facilitates the creation of invariant image features.

concepts.title: Local Amplitude
concepts.one_liner: Local amplitude is a measure of image power within a specific frequency bandwidth in a local neighborhood, computed using quadrature filters.
concepts.content:
Let $h(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ be band-pass filters in quadrature, and let $\ell_h(x,y)$ and $\ell_q(x,y)$ be the result of convolving the signal $\ell(x,y)$ with $h(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$, respectively. Then, the squared local amplitude is a measure of the image power within the frequency bandwidth of the filters in the local neighborhood of $(x,y)$:

$$a^2(x,y) = \ell_h ^2 (x,y) + \ell_q ^2 (x,y)$$

(see figure: Computation of localized amplitude. The input is filtered by a pair of quadrature Gabor filters. Each filter output is squared and the result is added.)

This process is similar to a two-layer convolutional neural network with two channels in the first layer, a squaring nonlinearity, and a sum in the second layer. Although the images $\ell_h(x,y)$ and $\ell_q(x,y)$ are band-pass, the resulting amplitude $a(x,y)$ is a low-pass image.
concepts.motivation_md: Local amplitude provides a way to detect the presence of specific textures or features regardless of their exact alignment, effectively acting as an 'energy detector' for specific frequencies.
concepts.recap_md:
- Local amplitude measures signal power in a specific frequency band and neighborhood.
- It is calculated as the square root of the sum of squared outputs from quadrature filters.
- While the inputs are band-pass, the resulting amplitude signal is low-pass.

concepts.title: Local Phase
concepts.one_liner: Local phase measures the angle between the real and imaginary components of a complex filter output, capturing local image structure.
concepts.content:
The local phase is a measure of the angle between the real and imaginary components (such as the cosine and sine components in complex Gabor filters):

$$\theta(x,y) = \angle \left[ \ell_h(x,y) + j \ell_q(x,y) \right]$$

where $\theta (x,y)$ is the instantaneous phase. This nonlinearity is sensitive to local image structure and has been used to estimate motion. Notably, this information is invariant to local changes in contrast.
concepts.motivation_md: Phase information is often more important than amplitude for identifying the location of features like edges. Because it is invariant to contrast, it allows vision systems to recognize structures under different lighting conditions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Local phase is the angle of the complex signal formed by quadrature filter outputs.
- It is sensitive to image structure but invariant to local contrast changes.
- It is a useful tool for tasks like motion estimation.

concepts.title: Filter Bank
concepts.one_liner: A filter bank is a collection of filters, each tuned to extract a different image feature, used to build an image representation.
concepts.content: A filter bank is a collection of filters, each tuned to extract a different image feature, and used to build an image representation.
concepts.motivation_md: Single filters can only detect specific features at specific scales or orientations. A filter bank allows a system to analyze an image across multiple scales and orientations simultaneously, providing a comprehensive description of the visual content.
concepts.recap_md:
- A filter bank consists of multiple filters tuned to different features.
- It is used to construct a multi-dimensional representation of an image.

concepts.title: Gabor Filter Bank
concepts.one_liner: A Gabor filter bank is a set of Gabor filters selective to different spatial frequencies that together cover the frequency domain.
concepts.content:
2D Gabor filters are selective in spatial frequency. It is very useful to work with sets of Gabor filters, each selective to a different spatial frequency so that they cover the full space of spatial frequencies.

(see figure: Examples of Gabor sets. Two different ways of tiling the frequency domain.)

There are different arrangements for Gabor filter banks. One approach uses a rectangular grid to sample the frequency domain, where all functions share the same $\sigma$. Another approach uses a polar arrangement where the Gaussian width $\sigma$ is proportional to the distance between the central frequency and the origin. This polar arrangement produces filters that are rotated and scaled versions of each other.
concepts.motivation_md: Gabor filter banks mimic the multi-scale, multi-orientation processing found in the primary visual cortex of mammals, making them highly effective for texture analysis and object recognition.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gabor filter banks tile the frequency domain to capture information at various scales and orientations.
- Rectangular arrangements use a fixed $\sigma$ across a grid.
- Polar arrangements scale $\sigma$ with frequency, creating self-similar rotated and scaled kernels.

concepts.title: Steerable Quadrature Pairs
concepts.one_liner: Steerable quadrature filters allow for arbitrary shifts in both orientation and phase by combining steerable basis functions with their Hilbert transform approximations.
concepts.content: As in the case of Gabor filters, it is useful to build quadrature pairs of steerable filters. Steerable-quadrature filters allow for arbitrary shifts both in orientation and in phase. We can design such filters by considering the second-order derivatives of a Gaussian with $\sigma^2=1/2$: $$\begin{split} g_{xx}(x,y) &= 0.9213(2x^2-1) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\ g_{xy}(x,y) &= 1.843 (x y) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\ g_{yy}(x,y) &= 0.9213(2y^2-1) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \end{split}$$ It is possible to get a good approximation to its Hilbert transform using a Gaussian times a third-order odd polynomial. The approximation to the Hilbert transform of $g_{xx}(x,y)$ is $h_{xx}(x,y) = -0.9780 (-2.254 x+x^3) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right)$, where $g_{xx}(x,y)$ and $h_{xx}(x,y)$ have the same spectral content but opposite phase. (see figure: Quadrature pair, $g_{xx} \left[n,m \right)$ and $h_{xx} \left[n,m \right]$. The filters are sampled in space and cropped into a window of $13\times13$ pixels.] To steer $h_{xx}(x,y)$ to an angle $\theta$, this approximation requires four basis functions: $h_{xx}$ and the three additional functions $h_2, h_3, h_4$: $$\begin{split} h_2(x,y) &= -0.9780(-0.7515+x^2) y \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\ h_3(x,y) &= -0.9780(-0.7515+y^2) x \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\ h_4(x,y) &= -0.9780 (-2.254 y+y^3) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \end{split}$$ These functions are optimized to be $x-y$ separable. The basis functions for steerability are not unique; for example, one can use separable filters ($g_{xx}, g_{xy}, g_{yy}$) or rotated versions of $g_{xx}$ at 0, 60, and 120 degrees to span the same space. (see figure: (a) Second derivative of Gaussian, $x-y$ separable steerable basis set. b) Approximation to Hilbert transform of second derivative of Gaussian, $x-y$ steerable basis set. (c) Nonseparable basis equivalent to (a). (d) Nonseparable basis set equivalent to (b).)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard steerable filters allow for rotation invariance, but adding a quadrature component (the Hilbert transform) provides phase invariance. This allows the filter to respond to local energy rather than specific phase alignments, which is essential for robust feature detection and oriented energy analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - Quadrature pairs consist of an even-phase filter (like a Gaussian derivative) and an odd-phase Hilbert transform approximation.

concepts.title: Oriented Energy Analysis
concepts.one_liner: Oriented energy is computed by summing the squared responses of quadrature filter pairs to detect image structures at specific angles independently of phase.
concepts.content: Oriented energy can be computed as a function of angle $\theta$ using the responses of seven basis filters: $$E(x,y,\theta) = g_{xx}(x,y,\theta)^2 + h_{xx}(x,y,\theta)^2$$ From these basis filter responses, polar plots of oriented energy can be formed to reveal local image structure. (see figure: (Polar plots of orientation energy as a function of angle, computed using $g_{xx}$, $h_{xx}$ filters. (a) Note the non-superposition of oriented energies near the junction of the two lines. (b)...) When multiple oriented structures exist within the passband, the squaring operation introduces cross-terms that appear as spurious spatial frequencies. This occurs because the combination of multiple structures is non-linear in the energy domain. These artifacts can be removed by spatially low-pass filtering (blurring) the squared oriented energy responses, resulting in cleaner energy plots at junctions. (see figure: Polar plots of orientation energy as a function of angle, computed using $g_{xx}$, $h_{xx}$ filters in two images.)
concepts.motivation_md: Oriented energy analysis allows us to detect the presence and orientation of lines and edges regardless of their phase (e.g., whether a line is light-on-dark or dark-on-light). It provides a way to characterize local image geometry through polar plots of energy versus angle.
concepts.recap_md: - Oriented energy is the sum of squared responses from a quadrature pair of steerable filters.

key_passage.text: E(x,y,θ) = g_{xx}(x,y,θ)^2 + h_{xx}(x,y,θ)^2

motivation.text: When there are two oriented structures within the passband of the quadrature pair filters, the sum of the energies of the individual structures is not the same as the energy of the sum of the structures. Because we're squaring to find the energies, the combination of multiple structures isn't linear.

concepts.title: Spatiotemporal Gabor Filters
concepts.one_liner: Spatiotemporal Gabor filters extend 2D Gabor functions to the $x-y-t$ domain to analyze signals moving through space and time.
concepts.content: Extending Gabor filters for motion analysis is a direct generalization of the $x-y$ 2D Gabor function to a $x-y-t$ 3D Gabor function. In one spatial dimension, an $x-t$ Gabor function is selective to signals translating at a specific speed, such as $v=1$. Its Fourier transform energy is contained along a Dirac line. (see figure: Space-time Gabor filters. (a) Cosine and sine $x$-$t$ Gabor filter, and (b) the sketch of its transfer function. (c) Sketch of the transfer function of a spatiotemporal Gabor filter in two spatial...) In two spatial dimensions, the $x-y-t$ Gabor filter is not selective to a unique velocity. Because the Fourier transform of a 2D moving signal $\ell(x-v_xt, y-v_yt)$ is contained within a Dirac plane, an infinite number of such planes can intersect the frequency response of a single Gabor filter. Consequently, a single Gabor filter cannot disambiguate the input velocity.
concepts.motivation_md: To analyze motion in video, we need filters that respond to changes in both space and time. Spatiotemporal Gabor filters provide a localized frequency analysis in the $x-y-t$ volume, serving as building blocks for motion and velocity estimation.
concepts.recap_md: - Spatiotemporal Gabor filters are 3D ($x, y, t$) extensions of spatial Gabor filters.

concepts.title: Velocity-Tuned Filters
concepts.one_liner: Velocity-tuned filters combine spatiotemporal quadrature pairs to identify the specific Fourier plane corresponding to a signal's motion.
concepts.content: Input velocity can be measured using quadrature pairs of oriented filters in space-time to find the orientation of strongest response. By sampling the space-time frequency domain with a set of Gabor filters, we can identify the plane in the Fourier domain that contains the input energy.  One possible architecture for velocity-selective units uses a first layer of space-time Gabor filters (cosine and sine) to compute phase-invariant amplitudes. These amplitude outputs are then combined to form different planes in the Fourier domain, creating velocity-selective outputs. A normalization layer may be added to divide each output by the sum of all amplitudes. Velocity is estimated by identifying the velocity-tuned unit with the strongest response. (see figure: Architecture to create velocity-selective units. In the first layer, cosine and sine filters are combined to create phase-invariant frequency-tuned outputs. In the second layer, the outputs of...)
concepts.motivation_md: While a single spatiotemporal filter is ambiguous regarding velocity, a bank of filters tuned to different spatiotemporal frequencies can collectively identify the specific plane in the Fourier domain that a moving object occupies, allowing for precise velocity estimation.
concepts.recap_md: - Velocity-tuned units are created by combining the amplitudes of multiple spatiotemporal Gabor filters.

concepts.title: Gabor Filter
concepts.one_liner: A Gabor filter is a localized oriented band-pass filter formed by the product of a Gaussian window and a sinusoidal wave.
concepts.content: Gabor filters provide localized image analysis by restricting the spatial support of sinusoidal basis functions using a Gaussian window. A complex Gabor function $\psi(x,y)$ is defined as: $$\psi(x,y;u_0,v_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma^2} \exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right)} \exp{ \left( j \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right) \right)}$$ The real and imaginary parts correspond to cosine and sine phase Gabor filters. The Fourier transform of a complex Gabor function is a Gaussian in the Fourier domain shifted with respect to the origin: $$\Psi(u,v; u_0,v_0) = \exp{ \left( - \left((u-u_0)^2 + (v-v_0)^2 \right) \frac{\sigma^2}{2} \right) }$$ The Gabor filter is an oriented band-pass filter. The parameter $\sigma$ sets the locality of the window of analysis, while $(u_0,v_0)$ adjust the orientation and frequency. These filters are similar to cortical receptive fields in the mammalian visual system. (see figure: Construction of a Gabor function. (a) Sine function. (b) Gaussian function. (c) Gabor function obtained as the product of (a) and (b).) (see figure: 2D Gabor functions. concepts.motivation_md: While the Fourier transform extracts frequency information globally, Gabor filters allow for the extraction of frequency and orientation information localized in space, mimicking biological vision systems.
concepts.recap_md: - Gabor filters are created by multiplying a sinusoid with a Gaussian window to achieve spatial localization.

key_passage.text: The product of the Gaussian and the sine wave (or a cosine wave) gives the function with the profile shown in fig-1D_gabor_function (c) called a Gabor filter. We can multiply a complex Fourier basis function, $\exp{ \left(j \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right) \right)}$, by a spatially localized 2D Gaussian window, $\exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$ to obtain a Gabor function, $\psi(x,y)$. The Gabor filter is an oriented band-pass filter.

motivation.text: For this information to be useful it needs to be localized. A good start for a localized image analysis is to restrict the spatial support of a sinusoidal basis function.

slots.example: Gabor filters provide localized image analysis by restricting the spatial support of sinusoidal basis functions using a Gaussian window. A complex Gabor function $\psi(x,y)$ is defined as: $$\psi(x,y;u_0,v_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma^2} \exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right)} \exp{ \left( j \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right) \right)}$$ The real and imaginary parts correspond to cosine and sine phase Gabor filters. The Fourier transform of a complex Gabor function is a Gaussian in the Fourier domain shifted with respect to the origin: $$\Psi(u,v; u_0,v_0) = \exp{ \left( - \left((u-u_0)^2 + (v-v_0)^2 \right) \frac{\sigma^2}{2} \right) }$$ The Gabor filter is an oriented band-pass filter. The parameter $\sigma$ sets the locality of the window of analysis, while $(u_0,v_0)$ adjust the orientation and frequency. prereq.rationale: Velocity-tuned units are constructed using a first layer of spatiotemporal Gabor filters to sample the space-time frequency domain.
The technique uses quadrature pairs (cosine and sine) to compute phase-invariant amplitudes necessary for velocity estimation.
The localization property is a fundamental characteristic of the Gabor function in both spatial and frequency domains.
Two filters are in quadrature if their impulse responses are Hilbert transform pairs.
An analytic signal is constructed by combining a real signal with its Hilbert transform.
Local amplitude is calculated by combining the outputs of two filters that are in quadrature phase.
Local phase is defined as the angle between the outputs of a quadrature filter pair.
A Gabor filter bank is a specific type of filter bank where the individual filters are Gabor functions.
A Gabor filter bank is a specific implementation of the general filter bank concept.
The Gabor transform is computed by applying Gabor filters with varying central frequencies.
Quadrature pairs are built by extending the steerable filter technique to include phase-shifted versions.
Creating quadrature pairs for steerable filters involves approximating the Hilbert transform of the basis filters.
Oriented energy is calculated by summing the squared outputs of steerable quadrature filter pairs.

overlay.rationale: Spatiotemporal Gabor filters are explicitly described as a direct generalization of 2D Gabor functions to the 3D x-y-t domain for motion analysis.
Velocity-tuned filters concretely demonstrate oriented energy analysis by finding the orientation of strongest response in the space-time Fourier domain.
The Steering Theorem provides the mathematical proof and quantitative requirements for the concept of orientation sampling.
The steering condition provides the formal mathematical requirement for a filter to be considered steerable.
The steering condition is the fundamental equation upon which the Steering Theorem is built.
The N+1 rule for polynomial filters is a specific application of the general Steering Theorem.
Using separable filters is a common optimization for implementing steerable filter banks efficiently.
Oriented energy is the squared local amplitude of the analytic signal formed by the quadrature filter pair.
